newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine opposition economists warn on deficits.
newsitem.headline: Argentine opposition economists warn on deficits.

text.p: Argentine opposition economists warned Friday of the dangers facing the country because of the combination of a high fiscal deficit and a growing shortfall in the balance of payments.

"In the context of an expansive period for the economy, with growth of eight percent, the fiscal deficit is very high and it is combined with a growing current account deficit," said Adolfo Sturzenegger, the economic advisor for the Action for the Republic -- the party set up by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo.
"And when the twin deficits are maintained economic management is complicated, particularly on the debt front," said Sturzenegger, speaking at a conference organized by the University of Tel Aviv.
Some analysts estimate a fiscal deficit of more than $5.0 billion this year, compared with $6.0 billion in 1996. The government predicts a deficit of $4.5 billion this year.

"The fiscal situation is delicate in spite of the high growth and even so there is neither military spending nor public investment," said Ricardo Lopez Murphy, a well known economist of the Radical Party.

Guillermo Calvo, a former advisor to Economy Minister Roque Fernandez, warned that the government should be in a position to take advantage of the cyclical upturn to retire debt through a fiscal surplus.
Even Carlos Rodriguez, Economic Policy Secretary at the Economy Minister, acknowledged the problem.

"I recognize that the fiscal deficit is a problem but let us be optimistic and see that the tendency is a falling deficit," said Rodriguez. "Fiscal balance was not achieved because the political pressures are great," he conceded.

Jose Luis Machinea, the economic advisor of the newly launched Radical Party/Frepaso opposition alliance, said the current account deficit is not so much a pressing problem as a concern because of its "tendency to grow constantly."
But Rodriguez said the current account "deficit is simply the logical consequence of surge in capital entering the country."
The current account deficit in 1997 is seen at $9.0 billion, or three percent of gross domestic product, up from $4.0 billion in 1996.
